analysis.one_liner: Bars internet providers from blocking, slowing, or charging extra for lawful websites and apps.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from its January 2007 introduction until the 110th Congress ended without action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written net neutrality rules into law. Internet providers could not block or slow down lawful websites, apps, or services, could not charge content companies for faster access, and could not force customers to buy a bundle of cable or phone services in order to get internet service. It preserved providers' ability to manage their networks, offer parental controls, and charge by speed or data amount. It also directed the FCC to set up a fast complaint process and to report annually to Congress on broadband competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses the internet. The bill guaranteed that subscribers could reach any lawful site or app at full speed, could attach any device that didn't harm the network, and could buy broadband on its own without renting a phone or cable bundle. Small websites and startups benefit because incumbents could not buy a speed advantage over them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and small web businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred broadband providers from blocking, interfering with, discriminating against, impairing, or degrading any person's ability to use lawful content, applications, or services over the internet.

It prohibited providers from charging content or application companies based on the type of content, and required that any content on their networks be treated on a reasonable and nondiscriminatory basis at least equal to the provider's own affiliated services.
It banned forced bundles: a provider could not require a customer to buy cable, phone, or IP voice service as a condition of buying broadband.

It required the FCC to set up a complaint process resolving violations within 90 days, gave the FCC power to award damages to complaining parties, and required annual reports to Congress on broadband content delivery and competition.

Providers retained clear allowances for network security, network management that does not distinguish content by source, parental controls and spam filters with customer opt-out, and tiered pricing based on bandwidth or data quantity.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — mainly large cable and telephone companies — lose the ability to block or throttle rivals, collect fees from websites for priority access, and force customers into service bundles. Industry groups argued at the time that such mandates would raise the cost of network upgrades.

drawbacks.text: The bill allowed providers to charge subscribers different prices based on bandwidth levels or actual data flow, so usage-based and speed-tiered pricing remained legal.
It carved out services regulated under title VI of the Communications Act regardless of the facilities used to transmit them, leaving a class of services outside the neutrality rules.

Broadband companies argued that net neutrality mandates would constrain network management flexibility and reduce incentives to invest in network upgrades; no vote was ever taken, so Congress never weighed that objection on the record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete for anyone who goes online: no blocking, no paid fast lanes, no forced bundles, with a fast FCC complaint path for violations. The main cost falls on broadband providers and, by their argument, could show up as slower network investment — though the bill explicitly preserved legitimate network management and tiered pricing, so the constraint is narrower than the industry's blanket objection suggests.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the Internet Freedom Preservation Act on January 9, 2007, with original cosponsors including Sens. Olympia Snowe, John Kerry, Barbara Boxer, Tom Harkin, Patrick Leahy, Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, and Ron Wyden.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill, including one Republican and one Independent.
The full action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call after the referral; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers were better off: they kept two more years of freedom to manage their networks, pursue paid delivery arrangements, and bundle services without the neutrality duties the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, who faced no new rules

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship at introduction.

for.name: Sens. Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 9 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Daniel Inouye)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no committee vote, and no report to the floor during the entire 110th Congress.

against.name: Large broadband providers (AT&T, Verizon, Comcast)
against.what_they_did: Opposed net neutrality legislation and lobbied Congress against mandates during the net neutrality debate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 11 cosponsors split 9 Democrats, 1 Republican (Sen. Snowe), and 1 Independent, and no recorded vote ever tested opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have barred blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization, and ended forced service bundles. Providers' interest in charging websites for speed and steering customers into bundles runs against subscribers' interest in open access at full speed.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and edge businesses (streaming services, startups, small websites)
industries.note: The bill guaranteed nondiscriminatory access to subscribers at speeds at least equal to the provider's own affiliated services, so incumbents could not buy a delivery advantage over newcomers.
